name: Inflation & Cost of Living: Who's to Blame?

archetypes.text: Kroger made $2.2 billion in profit last year while eggs are $8 a dozen. They're not passing along costs — they're padding margins and blaming inflation.
archetypes.subject: corporate grocery profit margins
archetypes.assertion: grocery chains are exploiting inflation to increase profit margins beyond cost pass-through

time_anchor.event: Kroger Q4 2024 earnings show record margins amid grocery price complaints

variations.text: Kroger posts $2.2B profit. Eggs are $8. They're not 'passing along costs' — they're printing money and calling it inflation.
$8 eggs and record grocery profits. At some point we gotta stop calling it inflation and start calling it what it is.
Friendly reminder that Kroger's profit margin INCREASED during 'inflation.' They didn't absorb costs. They added to them.

The Kroger/Albertsons merger antitrust case revealed internal docs showing executives discussing how inflation gave them 'cover' to raise prices beyond cost increases. This isn't conspiracy theory — it's in the court filings.

Economist here. The data on grocery margins is actually more nuanced than 'pure greed.' Input costs did rise (energy, labor, transport), but margins expanded ~15-20% beyond cost pass-through. It's both real inflation AND margin expansion.
Breaking down Kroger's earnings vs. what you're paying at the register. The gap between their costs and your prices tells the whole greedflation story.
I compared Kroger's ingredient costs to shelf prices across 50 products. The markup increase since 2021 is staggering — and it's not just 'supply chain.'

archetypes.text: Shrinkflation is the most insulting form of price increase. Same box, same price, 20% less product. The FTC is finally looking into it.
archetypes.subject: FTC shrinkflation investigation
archetypes.assertion: shrinkflation is a deceptive corporate practice that regulators should address

time_anchor.event: FTC announces focus on shrinkflation practices in consumer products

variations.text: My Gatorade bottle went from 32oz to 28oz at the same price. Companies are literally stealing from you in plain sight. Glad the FTC is finally on it.
Shrinkflation update: Doritos bags are now 9.25oz down from 10.5oz. Same price. Same shelf. Less chips. This is theft with better marketing.
The FTC going after shrinkflation is long overdue. Every company quietly shaving 15-20% off products while keeping prices the same is consumer fraud.

I've been tracking shrinkflation across 200+ products for 2 years. The median shrink is 14% with zero price reduction. Toilet paper is the worst offender — sheets per roll dropped 20-30% across every major brand.

The FTC investigation into shrinkflation is a good start but misses the bigger point: we need standardized unit pricing displayed as prominently as the sticker price. Most consumers don't do oz-by-oz math in the aisle.
I bought the same 50 grocery items from 2019 and 2024 and measured every single one. The shrinkflation results will genuinely shock you.
The FTC is finally investigating shrinkflation — here's why it took so long and what it actually means for the brands doing it.

archetypes.text: The Fed held rates too long trying to be heroes and now we're paying for it. 5.5% for over a year crushed small businesses while doing nothing about grocery prices.
archetypes.subject: Federal Reserve rate policy impact
archetypes.assertion: the Fed's prolonged high interest rates damaged small businesses without meaningfully reducing consumer prices

time_anchor.event: Fed holds federal funds rate at 5.25-5.50% through eight consecutive meetings

variations.text: The Fed kept rates at 5.5% for a YEAR. Small businesses closed. Housing froze. And groceries are still expensive. Explain to me how this worked.
Powell held rates at 5.5% to fight inflation but the inflation people actually feel — food, insurance, rent — didn't budge. Mission accomplished?
Small business owner here. 5.5% rates for 14 months meant I couldn't expand, couldn't hire, couldn't refinance. Meanwhile Kroger's profits went up. Cool system.

The Fed's rate hold strategy was textbook monetarism applied to a largely supply-side inflation problem. Raising rates doesn't fix avian flu egg shortages or insurance actuarial recalculations. It just makes credit expensive for everyone else.

The irony of Fed policy: they held rates at 5.5% for over a year, which did cool demand-side inflation, but the sticky categories people complain about most (shelter, food, insurance) are driven by supply constraints that rate policy can't touch.
The Fed held rates at 5.5% for over a year. Here's who actually got hurt, who benefited, and why the inflation you feel didn't go away.
Breaking down 14 months of 5.5% interest rates: small businesses paid the price while the corporations causing price increases barely noticed.

archetypes.text: The September rate cut was the right call. CPI is trending down, labor market is cooling, and Powell finally read the room. Soft landing is real.
archetypes.subject: Fed September 2024 rate cut
archetypes.assertion: the Fed's September 2024 rate cut was appropriately timed as inflation cools

time_anchor.event: Federal Reserve cuts rates 50 basis points in September FOMC meeting

variations.text: Fed cuts 50bps. CPI trending to 2%. Unemployment still under 4.5%. The soft landing actually happened and nobody wants to admit it.
The September rate cut is going to age well. Inflation cooling, jobs holding, no recession. Powell stuck the landing.
Everyone who said the Fed was going to crash the economy into a recession — where are you now? 50bp cut, markets stable, inflation down. This is the soft landing.

Credit where it's due: the 50bp September cut was well-timed. Core PCE at 2.7%, trending right direction, labor market softening but not breaking. The historical comparison to Volcker is lazy — this is much more surgical.

Hot take that shouldn't be hot: the Fed did a genuinely good job navigating post-pandemic inflation. We got CPI from 9.1% to under 3% without a recession. That's historically unprecedented for this scale of price shock.
The Fed just cut rates for the first time in 4 years. Here's what it means for your mortgage, your savings account, and whether the 'soft landing' is really happening.
Analyzing the September rate cut decision: why 50 basis points, why now, and what the data actually tells us about where inflation is headed.

archetypes.text: Wages are up 4% and prices are up 20% since 2020. Do the math. You're not imagining it — you're objectively poorer than you were four years ago.
archetypes.subject: real wage purchasing power decline
archetypes.assertion: wage growth has not kept pace with cumulative price increases since 2020

time_anchor.event: BLS data shows cumulative CPI increase ~20% since January 2020 vs ~17% cumulative wage growth

variations.text: Wages up 4% this year. Prices up 20% since 2020. That's not a raise. That's a pay cut with better PR.
They keep saying wages are growing faster than inflation NOW. Cool. But I lost 20% of my purchasing power over 4 years. I'm still underwater.
Annual wage growth beating annual inflation doesn't mean you've recovered from 4 years of price increases. The cumulative gap is real and no one in DC wants to talk about it.

The 'wages are outpacing inflation' headline is technically true on a year-over-year basis but deeply misleading. Cumulative price level since Jan 2020 is up ~20%. Cumulative nominal wage growth is ~17%. Real purchasing power is still negative for most workers.

I make $15k more than I did in 2020. My rent is $600/mo higher, groceries cost 25% more, and my car insurance doubled. I'm saving less money on a higher salary. The 'wage growth beats inflation' narrative ignores the cumulative gap.
I calculated my actual purchasing power from 2020 vs today using my real expenses. Even with a 20% raise, I'm worse off. Here are the exact numbers.
The real story behind 'wages are beating inflation' — why the year-over-year stat hides a much uglier truth about American purchasing power.

archetypes.text: Minimum wage workers in 2024 have less buying power than minimum wage workers in 1968. Adjusted for inflation, $7.25 today is worth less than $1.60 was then.
archetypes.subject: federal minimum wage purchasing power comparison
archetypes.assertion: the federal minimum wage has declined in real terms to below 1968 levels

time_anchor.event: Federal minimum wage remains at $7.25 for 15th consecutive year

variations.text: Federal minimum wage: $7.25 since 2009. Fifteen years. Meanwhile everything costs 40% more. This country is not serious.
The 1968 minimum wage of $1.60 is worth more than $7.25 today adjusted for inflation. We went backwards. Literally backwards.
$7.25/hr in 2024. That's $15,080/year before taxes. Median rent is $1,400/mo. You do the math and tell me this is a functioning system.

It's genuinely insane that we're in year 15 of a $7.25 federal minimum wage. Even states that have raised their own minimums to $15 are now watching that become insufficient. The purchasing power decay is relentless.

A comparison I run annually: the 1968 minimum wage ($1.60) in 2024 dollars is roughly $14.15. The current federal minimum is $7.25. American minimum wage workers have lost 49% of their purchasing power relative to 1968.
I tried to live on $7.25 an hour for a month in 3 different US cities. Here's what happened and why the federal minimum wage is a policy failure.
Comparing what minimum wage bought you in 1968 vs 2024 — the numbers tell a story politicians don't want to hear.

archetypes.text: CPI says inflation is 3.2%. My car insurance went up 22%, groceries are up 25% since 2021, and my rent jumped $200/mo. What exactly is CPI measuring?
archetypes.subject: CPI accuracy and consumer experience gap
archetypes.assertion: official CPI figures understate the inflation experienced by typical consumers

time_anchor.event: October 2024 CPI report shows 3.2% annual inflation amid consumer complaints about higher experienced costs

variations.text: CPI: 3.2%. My actual life: insurance +22%, groceries +25%, rent +15%. I don't live in the CPI basket.
Government says inflation is 3.2% and I genuinely want to know who is experiencing 3.2% inflation. Because it's not me, my family, or anyone I know.
CPI counts a TV getting cheaper as offsetting your groceries getting more expensive. That's not how budgets work. That's how statistics lie.

The CPI methodology is sound for what it measures (broad urban consumer basket), but it fails catastrophically as a measure of 'felt inflation.' Shelter has a massive lag due to OER methodology, food and energy are volatile, and insurance/healthcare are weighted low relative to household experience.

I tracked every dollar I spent in 2023 vs 2024. My personal inflation rate was 11.2%. CPI said 3.2%. The gap is explained by: car insurance (+22%), health insurance (+18%), groceries (+8%), and childcare (+12%). These categories hit harder than CPI weights suggest.
I broke down exactly how CPI is calculated and why it doesn't match what you're paying. The methodology isn't wrong — but it might not measure YOUR inflation.
Why the government says inflation is 3% while your budget says it's 15%. The CPI measurement gap explained.

archetypes.text: The 'vibecession' is real. Economy is technically fine by the numbers but nobody feels fine. Maybe the numbers are wrong or maybe 'fine' doesn't mean what it used to.
archetypes.subject: vibecession consumer sentiment disconnect
archetypes.assertion: negative consumer sentiment persists despite positive macroeconomic indicators

time_anchor.event: University of Michigan consumer sentiment survey remains depressed despite GDP growth and low unemployment

variations.text: GDP is up. Unemployment is low. Stock market is at ATH. And everyone feels broke. The vibecession isn't vibes — it's price levels.
We really coined 'vibecession' instead of admitting the economic metrics might not capture lived reality anymore.
The economy is fine. The economy is fine. The economy is fine. My grocery bill disagrees but sure, the economy is fine.

The vibecession debate comes down to this: economists measure rates of change (inflation falling), consumers experience levels (prices are still 20% higher). Both are correct. The disconnect is methodological, not perceptual.

I think the vibecession is explained by three factors: (1) cumulative price shock hasn't reversed, (2) housing costs consume a larger share of income, (3) social media amplifies worst-case comparisons. It's not irrational — it's asymmetric exposure to real pressures.
The 'vibecession' explained: why Americans feel terrible about an economy that looks great on paper — and which side is actually right.
Economists say the economy is strong. Consumers say they're struggling. I dug into the data to figure out who's right about the vibecession.

archetypes.text: Biden keeps saying he brought inflation down from 9% to 3%. He didn't bring prices down. Prices are permanently 20% higher. 'Slower inflation' isn't cheaper groceries.
archetypes.subject: political framing of inflation reduction
archetypes.assertion: claiming credit for reduced inflation rate is misleading when price levels remain elevated

time_anchor.event: Biden administration repeatedly cites inflation rate decline in 2024 campaign messaging

variations.text: Biden: 'We brought inflation down from 9% to 3%.' Bro you didn't bring PRICES down. Everything is still 20% more expensive. Slower robbery is still robbery.
'Inflation is coming down' is the most gaslighting phrase in American politics. My grocery bill didn't come down. My rent didn't come down. Nothing came DOWN.
Inflation rate ≠ prices. Prices went up 20% and stayed there. Saying inflation is down is like saying the bleeding slowed while you're still bleeding.

The rate vs level distinction is genuinely one of the most consequential communication failures in recent economic policy. When politicians say 'inflation is down,' voters hear 'prices are falling.' Prices are not falling. They rose ~20% and plateaued. Both statements are true and they describe very different realities.

The Biden administration's inflation messaging was a textbook case of correct statistics, wrong framing. Year-over-year CPI did fall from 9.1% to ~3%. But that doesn't mean prices dropped. Consumers experienced a permanent upward price shift, and no amount of rate-decline messaging addresses that.
Politicians keep saying inflation is down. Here's why that doesn't mean what you think it means — and why your grocery bill proves the point.
The biggest lie in economic messaging: 'We brought inflation down.' What that actually means vs what people hear — explained with real numbers.

archetypes.text: Trump says he'll fix grocery prices on day one. No president controls grocery prices. This is the same empty promise from a different direction.
archetypes.subject: Trump grocery price promise
archetypes.assertion: presidential promises to directly lower grocery prices are unrealistic regardless of party

time_anchor.event: Trump campaign promises to lower grocery prices in first term during 2024 campaign

variations.text: Trump promising to lower grocery prices day one is the same energy as Biden saying he fixed inflation. Neither president has a grocery price lever in the Oval Office.
No president — Trump, Biden, anyone — controls what eggs cost at Walmart. Promising to 'fix grocery prices' is pandering and everyone should call it out.
The 'I'll fix grocery prices' promise from both sides is exhausting. Presidents don't set food prices. Supply chains, corporate margins, and global commodities do.

As an agricultural economist: no US president can meaningfully control grocery prices through executive action. Food prices are driven by global commodity markets, energy costs, labor markets, supply chain efficiency, and corporate pricing decisions. The levers available to a president are indirect and slow-acting.

Both Trump and Biden promised to address grocery prices and both were/are making promises they can't keep. The president has essentially no direct control over consumer food prices. They can influence ag subsidies, trade policy, and antitrust enforcement — none of which produce quick results.
Can any president actually lower grocery prices? I asked economists from both sides of the aisle and the honest answer is... complicated.
Trump promises to fix food prices. Biden says he already did. Here's why neither statement holds up to scrutiny — and who actually controls what you pay.

archetypes.text: The $18 Big Mac went viral but the real story is a McDonald's combo meal costs $15-18 in most cities now. Fast food used to be the cheap option. It's not anymore.
archetypes.subject: fast food price escalation
archetypes.assertion: fast food has become unaffordable relative to its historical positioning as a budget option

time_anchor.event: $18 Big Mac receipt goes viral on social media, McDonald's CEO addresses pricing concerns

variations.text: The $18 Big Mac was an outlier. The $15 Big Mac combo is not. Fast food is no longer fast food prices and that's the real problem.
Went to McDonald's and a Quarter Pounder meal was $16.89. At that price I'll just go to a sit-down restaurant. Fast food broke its own value proposition.
McDonald's, Chipotle, Wendy's — they all quietly became $15-18/meal restaurants. The 'dollar menu' era is dead and it's not coming back.

The fast food pricing crisis is an underrated inflation indicator. McDonald's was designed as affordable food for working people. When a Big Mac meal costs $16-18, it means the entire pricing structure of the American food economy has shifted upward permanently.

I keep a spreadsheet of fast food prices and a McDonald's Big Mac combo in my area (suburban Midwest) went from $8.29 in 2019 to $14.69 in 2024. That's 77% in 5 years. CPI food-away-from-home says 28%. The gap is real.
I priced out the exact same McDonald's order from 2019 vs 2024 in 10 cities. The average increase is 72%. Here's why fast food isn't fast food anymore.
The death of cheap fast food: how McDonald's, Chipotle, and Wendy's all became $15-18 per meal — and what it says about inflation.

archetypes.text: Car insurance went up 22% this year and nobody is talking about it. Not groceries, not gas — insurance is the silent budget killer in 2024.
archetypes.subject: auto insurance cost spike
archetypes.assertion: car insurance cost increases are a major underreported contributor to consumer financial pressure

time_anchor.event: BLS data shows auto insurance CPI component up 22.2% year-over-year, highest since 1976

variations.text: Everyone's talking about egg prices. Nobody's talking about car insurance being up 22% in one year. My premium went from $180/mo to $240/mo for the same coverage.
Car insurance: +22%. Home insurance: +12%. Health insurance: +8%. These aren't optional expenses. You can't 'stop buying' insurance. This is the inflation that actually breaks budgets.
The car insurance increases are INSANE and I feel like I'm the only person screaming about this. 22% in a year. For mandatory insurance. That you can't opt out of.

The auto insurance spike is driven by three things: (1) higher vehicle repair costs due to tech-heavy cars, (2) increased accident severity, (3) insurers catching up after underpricing during COVID. It's a structural repricing, not temporary inflation. Premiums aren't coming back down.

I'm an insurance adjuster and can explain the 22% increase: modern cars cost 40% more to repair than 5 years ago (sensors, cameras, aluminum bodies). The industry underpriced risk during COVID and is now correcting. This isn't corporate greed — it's actuarial math. Rates will plateau but not decrease.
Your car insurance went up 22% this year and here's exactly why — plus what you can actually do to lower your premium right now.
The insurance inflation crisis nobody is talking about: auto, home, and health insurance are up double digits and there's no end in sight.

archetypes.text: I did the 2019 vs 2024 grocery comparison everyone's doing. Same 30 items, same store. $97 in 2019, $141 in 2024. That's 45% in five years. CPI says food is up 25%. Someone's math is wrong.
archetypes.subject: personal grocery cost tracking vs CPI
archetypes.assertion: individual grocery cost tracking shows price increases significantly exceeding official CPI food inflation figures

time_anchor.event: Viral trend of 2019 vs 2024 grocery receipt comparisons across social media platforms

variations.text: 2019 grocery receipt: $97. 2024 same items same store: $141. That's 45%. CPI food says 25%. I trust my receipt.
Join the 2019 vs 2024 grocery receipt challenge. Buy the exact same items. Post both receipts. Let's see what real inflation looks like.
Did the grocery comparison thing. 30 items. Same Walmart. $97 → $141. Tell me again that inflation is only 3%.

The grocery receipt comparisons going viral are interesting but methodologically flawed. CPI tracks a rotating basket with substitution effects (chicken→turkey if chicken spikes). Personal receipts track fixed items. Both are valid perspectives — CPI measures 'cost of living at similar quality,' receipts measure 'cost of the same stuff.'

I did a rigorous version of the grocery receipt comparison: same 40 items, same store, same brands, using my actual receipts from January 2020 vs January 2024. Total increase: 38%. BLS CPI food-at-home for the same period: 25%. The gap is mostly explained by above-average increases in eggs (+89%), butter (+32%), and bread (+36%).
I recreated my exact 2019 grocery haul in 2024 with camera proof of every price. The total difference will make you rethink every inflation headline you've read.
The viral grocery receipt challenge: I compared 50 items from 2019 vs 2024 at the same store. The CPI doesn't capture what I found.
I asked 20 families to recreate their 2019 grocery trips in 2024. The average increase was 42% — way above official numbers. Here's why.

archetypes.text: Egg prices hitting $8 is not 'inflation.' It's avian flu killing 100 million birds and one company — Cal-Maine — controlling 20% of supply and posting record profits during a shortage.
archetypes.subject: egg price causes and market concentration
archetypes.assertion: egg price spikes are driven by avian flu supply shocks and market concentration, not general inflation

time_anchor.event: Egg prices spike above $8/dozen amid avian flu resurgence and Cal-Maine Foods reports record quarterly profits

variations.text: $8 eggs. Cal-Maine controls 20% of the market and just posted record profits. This isn't inflation. It's a monopoly exploiting a bird flu crisis.
Avian flu killed 100M birds. Cal-Maine posted RECORD profits. They're not passing along costs — they're profiting from a crisis. $8 eggs isn't supply and demand. It's extraction.
Stop saying '$8 eggs = inflation.' $8 eggs = avian flu + market concentration + a company choosing to maximize margins during a shortage. Very different things.

The egg pricing situation is a perfect case study in how multiple factors compound: (1) genuine supply shock from avian flu killing 100M+ birds, (2) market concentration with Cal-Maine holding ~20% share, (3) inelastic demand (people don't stop buying eggs), (4) no rapid supply recovery mechanism. Cal-Maine's record profits during the shortage are the greedflation element.

Former ag industry analyst here. The egg price story is more nuanced than 'greedflation.' Avian flu did destroy supply. But Cal-Maine's margins expanded beyond cost pass-through because concentrated markets allow price-setting behavior during supply shocks. Both supply and market structure are the problem.
Why do eggs cost $8? It's not just inflation — it's avian flu, market concentration, and one company making record profits from a crisis. The full breakdown.
Cal-Maine Foods posted record profits while you're paying $8 for eggs. I traced the money from farm to shelf to explain exactly where your money goes.
